hook_text: A security gate's arms never change length — but the space inside them vanishes as it closes. That's the whole area rule.
clip_script: Look at a trellis security gate — the concertina kind. Take one cell of it: two arms, hinged at a corner. Open the gate so the arms stand at ninety degrees, and that cell traps its biggest possible space. Now slide the gate closed. The arms never change length — but the space between them shrinks, and shrinks, until it's gone. THAT is the area rule for any triangle: half, times one side, times the other side, times sine of the angle between them. Sine is the squash factor. At ninety degrees sine is one — no squash, maximum area, and the formula turns back into half base times height. Squash the angle down to nothing and sine hits zero — flat arms, no triangle, no area. So when an exam gives you two sides of a plot and the angle where they meet, you don't need any perpendicular height. Half, times side, times side, times sine of the wedged-in angle. One warning: the angle MUST sit between your two sides. Touch the two sides on your sketch — the corner where your fingers meet is the only angle allowed in the formula.
visual_style: A yellow trellis gate concertinas open and shut in a township doorway; one parallelogram cell glows, morphs into a triangle, and its shaded area swells and collapses as the hinge angle changes, with sine values ticking on screen.
pacing: Slow squeeze of the gate, hard stop at ninety degrees, quick collapse to zero, brisk formula recap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take the area and sine rules into any triangle the exam throws at you.
